title: What is the Actor model as used by Akka? Explain private state, asynchronous immutable messages, the mailbox, how it eliminates shared mutable state, and the trade-offs versus locks.
keyPoints: An actor owns private mutable state that no one else can touch.
Communication is only by sending asynchronous immutable messages into the actor's mailbox.
The actor processes one message at a time, so internal mutations are automatically safe without locks.
Akka schedules millions of lightweight actors over a small thread pool.
Eliminates shared mutable state: no locks, no data races, no deadlocks by design.
Trade-offs: message-passing latency, eventual ordering, unbounded mailboxes need backpressure, harder debugging.
Actors shine for stateful, event-driven systems; a short critical section may still be cleaner with a lock.

s1_definition.oneliner: An actor owns private state, receives asynchronous immutable messages into a mailbox, and processes them one at a time, so shared mutable state and locks disappear entirely.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Actor** – an object with private mutable state, a mailbox, and a message handler.
- **Private state** – no other thread or actor can read or write it; the only interface is messages.
- **Immutable messages** – data sent between actors must be immutable so sending is safe across threads.
- **Mailbox** – per-actor queue of pending messages; the actor processes one at a time, in order.
- **Akka** – JVM implementation scheduling millions of lightweight actors over a small thread pool.
- **Trade-offs** – message latency, eventual ordering, unbounded mailboxes, harder debugging.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine each account at National Bank of India has its own dedicated clerk who alone can touch that account's ledger. If you want something done, you drop a written request into the clerk's in-tray (mailbox). The clerk handles one request at a time. Since only one clerk touches each ledger, two people can never corrupt the balance.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Actor Model:

  ┌──────────────┐   message   ┌──────────────┐
  │  Sender      │──────────▶ │  Mailbox     │
  │ (async, fire │             │  [msg1]      │
  │  and forget) │             │  [msg2]      │
  └──────────────┘             │  [msg3]      │
                               └──────┬───────┘
                                      │
                                      ▼
                               ┌──────────────┐
                               │  Actor       │
                               │  Private     │
                               │  State:      │
                               │  balance=50K │
                               │              │
                               │  Processes   │
                               │  one msg at  │
                               │  a time      │
                               └──────────────┘

  No locks needed: only one thread touches the state.
  No data races: state is private.
  No deadlocks: no locks to order incorrectly.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Actor model gives each actor private state, asynchronous immutable messages, and a mailbox processed one at a time. This eliminates shared mutable state, so there are no locks, no data races, and no deadlocks by design. Akka schedules millions of actors over a small thread pool.

The trade-offs are real: message latency, eventual ordering, unbounded mailboxes need backpressure, and async flows are harder to debug. For a short critical section, a lock can be cleaner.

At National Bank of India we modeled each account as an actor so deposits and withdrawals from many channels are serialized by the mailbox, removing locks entirely.

Remember one sentence: an actor owns private state and processes immutable messages one at a time, eliminating shared mutable state so locks, data races, and deadlocks disappear by design.
